archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (possession-driven)
archetype.definition: A team that leads the league in both 5-on-5 shot and chance share but sits merely in the top third in goal differential, because its goalies and its finishers have given back much of that edge.

report.headline: The league's best five-on-five team is being held back by its own crease
report.take:
New Jersey is 7-4-0 and seventh on the site's Teams tab, which is a fine start. It also undersells what has happened on the ice. The Devils rank first in the league in both xGF % (61.5%) and CF % (60%). They put 32.1 shots on goal a game, second in the league, and allow 23.8, seventh. That is an 11-game sample, but tilting the ice this hard across a full month usually reflects how a team is built rather than a run of luck. The forwards grade A- and the blueline A, and the possession numbers are spread across the lineup. Every listed skater has an xGF % above .530, and Bratt, Evangelista, Jack Hughes and Gritsyuk are all above .650.

The gap between that dominance and a Goal Diff / GP of 0.36, 11th in the league, sits almost entirely at the two ends of the rink. In goal, the Devils have a D- grade, a team GSAx of -4.9 (27th) and a combined .882 save percentage (25th). Neither Jake Allen (-3.5 GSAx) nor Nico Daws (-2.3) has been even average. At the other end, the skaters are shooting 10.1% against a league average of 11.3%; Timo Meier has one goal on 46 shots. Add a penalty kill at 74.1% (23rd) and you get a 5-on-5 PDO of 97.7 attached to the best underlying team in the league.

The Pts vs Goal Diff number is +0.5, so the record is not built on close-game luck. If anything, the record understates the team. The concern is that goaltending has been a recurring problem rather than a one-month dip. Last season ended with a -3.5 GSAx and a 97.1 PDO, and 2023-24 sat at -11.4. Only 2024-25, at +23.3, showed what this core looks like with a goalie behind it. So the real question is whether Allen and Daws can get back to roughly league average, not whether they will get hot.

The last five games hint at what that looks like: 4-1-0, 20 goals for and 10 against, with the defense allowing nearly a goal a game less than its season rate. Even with these goalies, the current pace works out to 52 wins and 104 points. If the save percentage rises toward the league's .892 while the shot share holds, this becomes a team that should push Carolina for the Metropolitan lead.

strengths.title: League-best five-on-five control
strengths.body: New Jersey owns both the largest share of expected goals and the largest share of shot attempts in the league. The forward group combined for 229 shots, and the blueline adds volume led by Luke Hughes (32 shots) and Dougie Hamilton (28). Because this comes from territorial play rather than shooting luck, it is the part of the profile most likely to last.

strengths.title: Deep, productive top six
strengths.body: Jack Hughes drives the attack with 12 points and a .656 xGF %. Hischier ranks 10th among centers on the site, and Bratt ranks 13th among left wingers. Arseny Gritsyuk leads the team with 6 goals, and Evangelista has 7 points in 8 games. The offense does not depend on one line, which is why the forwards grade A-.

strengths.title: A blueline that suppresses shots
strengths.body: The defense grades A. Luke Hughes logs 24 minutes a night and ranks 10th of 250 defensemen on the site, while Pesce and Hamilton both rank inside the top 30. Opponents manage only 23.8 shots a game, well under the league's 26.9. That structure is what keeps the shaky goaltending from costing even more.

concerns.title: Goaltending is giving goals back
concerns.body: Both goalies are below expected: Allen at -3.5 GSAx and Daws at -2.3, for a team mark of -4.9 that ranks 27th. The combined .882 save percentage is a full point below the league average, and this franchise has had a below-zero GSAx in three of its last five seasons. Some improvement is likely because the shots they face are limited, but expecting average play is the optimistic case, not the baseline.

concerns.title: Leaky penalty kill
concerns.body: The PK is killing 74.1%, 23rd in the league and well under the league's 78.3%. Every recent Devils season held the kill at 79% or better. That makes this look like a small sample made worse by poor goaltending, not a structural flaw, but it matters in a week against a Vegas power play ranked ninth.

concerns.title: Opposing defensemen are scoring
concerns.body: Defensemen score far more against New Jersey than their own averages predict. That gap ranks 27th, and blueliners take a much larger share of the points against the Devils than they do league-wide. This fits a team that pens opponents in their zone and gets beaten on point shots and through traffic. That is a goalie problem as much as a coverage one.

trend.note: After losing three of the first four games, including a 0-6 loss on Long Island, New Jersey went 6-1 with three straight wins to close October. Over the last five it doubled its opponents' scoring, 20 goals to 10.

weekAhead.headline: Three road games, starting with the league's stingiest defense
weekAhead.body:
It is a western road trip with a back-to-back up front: Dallas on the 27th, Colorado the next night, then Vegas on the 30th. Dallas is the hardest test on the schedule. The Stars are fourth on the site, allow the fewest goals and shots in the league, and have held centers, wingers and defensemen furthest under their averages. Their goalies have a .928 save percentage and a +9.9 GSAx. Dallas does not out-chance teams the way New Jersey does, with a 53.2% xGF %, so the Devils should control territory. Turning that control into goals against an A+ crease is the problem.

Colorado is the best chance to cash in. The Devils beat the Avalanche 4-3 at home on Oct. 20, and the Avalanche are giving up 28.3 shots a game with a C- goaltending group. They also allow the 28th-worst production to both centers and defensemen relative to expectation. Colorado's 105.4 PDO and 14% shooting point to an offense running hot, so on the second night of a back-to-back New Jersey's own goalie has to hold up. Vegas has an A-grade forward group but a kill at just 67.7%, so New Jersey's middling power play gets a real opening. Taking two of three on this trip would be a good week.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume vs. Dallas goaltending
keyMatchups.body: New Jersey's 32.1 shots a game meet the league's best save percentage, .928. Dallas wins by preventing goals rather than by dominating play. If the Devils can't solve its goalies, a game they control could still end in a 2-1 loss.

keyMatchups.title: Hughes and Hischier vs. Colorado's middle
keyMatchups.body: Colorado's defense gives centers well more than their averages predict, ranking 28th, and it allows 28.3 shots a game. That is a matchup tailored for Jack Hughes and Hischier.

keyMatchups.title: Special teams in Vegas
keyMatchups.body: Vegas kills just 67.7% of penalties, 28th in the league, while its own power play runs at 24.4%. New Jersey's 74.1% kill faces a real test, and its 20.6% power play faces a soft one. This game could be decided by which unit wins that exchange.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts the second night of the Dallas–Colorado back-to-back, and whether either Allen or Daws posts a save percentage near league average on this trip.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is real. A team that leads the league in both shot share and expected-goal share across a month, with A-range grades at forward and on defense, should keep winning the territorial battle. The finishing should also drift up from 10.1% toward the league's 11.3%, since the chances are there. Those two things should keep New Jersey comfortably in the playoff picture and likely near the top of the Metropolitan.

Goaltending sets how high the ceiling goes. If the save percentage stays in the .880s, the Devils are a 95-100 point team that loses too many games it controls. If Allen and Daws reach league average, the possession edge points to something like the 2022-23 team's 112 points. My middle case has the crease improving only partly, landing around 100 points.
swingFactors: Whether Allen or Daws stabilizes at league-average save %
Penalty kill recovering to recent-season levels

confidence.note: Eleven games is a small sample, but the possession signals are large and consistent across the roster.
